title: C# Questions & Answers - Introduction of Properties
sourceFile: Properties Basics - C# Questions & Answers - Sanfoundry.html
description: This section of our 1000+ C# multiple choice questions focuses on properties introduction in C# Programming Language.

questions.question: Which of the following is an INCORRECT statement about properties in C#?

options.text: Every property must always consist of both 'get' and 'set' accessors
A property cannot be defined as read-only or write-only
Properties can be used to encapsulate data members of a class
Properties are called like fields but execute code like methods

questions.explanation: In C#, properties are very flexible. You can define a property with only a 'get' accessor (read-only) or only a 'set' accessor (write-only). Therefore, saying it *cannot* be read or write only is false.

questions.question: What is the advantage of using properties instead of making data members public?

options.text: Properties can have different access levels for get and set
Properties allow validation of values before they are assigned to a variable
Properties promote encapsulation by hiding the internal representation of data
All of the mentioned

questions.explanation: Properties provide a powerful layer of abstraction. They allow you to add logic (like validation or logging) during data access without changing the class's public interface.

questions.question: In which of the following types can properties be declared in C#?

options.text: Class
Struct
Interface
All of the mentioned

questions.explanation: C# supports properties in classes, structures (structs), and interfaces. Interfaces define the property signature that implementing classes must provide.

questions.question: Which access modifiers can be used with C# properties?

options.text: private
public
protected internal
All of the mentioned

questions.explanation: Properties follow the same access modifier rules as other class members (public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, and private protected).

questions.question: Which of the following is true about write-only properties?

options.text: They only contain a 'set' accessor
The values assigned to them cannot be read back through the same property
They are useful for sensitive information like passwords
All of the mentioned

questions.explanation: A write-only property provides a way to send data to an object without allowing external code to retrieve that specific data back through the property getter.

questions.question: In class 'Maths', if you want the statement 'obj.Sum = 10' to cause a compile-time error, how should you declare the 'Sum' property?

options.text: Declare it with both get and set accessors
Declare it with only a 'get' accessor
Declare it as a static property
None of the mentioned

questions.explanation: A property without a 'set' accessor is read-only. Any attempt to assign a value to it will result in a compiler error.

questions.question: In class 'Maths', if you want the statement 'Console.WriteLine(obj.Sum)' to cause a compile-time error, how should you declare the 'Sum' property?

options.text: Declare it with only a 'get' accessor
Declare it with only a 'set' accessor
Declare it with a private 'set' accessor
All of the mentioned

questions.explanation: A property without a 'get' accessor is write-only. Attempting to read its value will result in a compiler error.

questions.question: To make the following code snippet work, how must the property be defined?

options.text: Declare the property with both 'get' and 'set' accessors
Declare it as an auto-implemented property
Declare it as a public field
Both A and B are valid solutions

questions.explanation: To both assign a value and read it back, the property needs both accessors. This can be done with a backing field (Option A) or using shorthand auto-property syntax (Option B).

questions.question: If the class 'Math' has an instance property 'Add' with both get and set accessors, which code is correct?

options.text: Math.Add = 20;
Math m = new Math(); m.Add = 10;
Console.WriteLine(Math.Add);
None of the mentioned

questions.explanation: Instance properties require an object instance created with 'new' to be accessed. You cannot call them via the class name like static properties.

questions.question: If the class 'Math' has an 'Add' property with only a 'get' accessor, which of the following statements is valid?

options.text: Math m = new Math(); m.Add = 10;
Math m = new Math(); m.Add += 20;
Math m = new Math(); int i = m.Add;
Math.Add = 20;

questions.explanation: Since the property is read-only (only 'get'), you can retrieve its value and assign it to a variable, but you cannot assign a new value to the property itself.
